Lula, who is seeking his fourth term after winning back the presidency in 2022, has defended his government's above-inflation minimum wage increases and stressed that his administration helped millions of Brazilians to escape hunger. The president said the younger Bolsonaro "is like students studying for college entrance exams. They can memorize things, but they can't learn." He also said that "in the gated community where Bolsonaro lives, people don't go hungry." Bolsonaro responded by saying food prices for Brazilians rose during Lula's administration, and he criticized a tax reform approved by the current government, projecting the new rules would raise the tax burden on consumers. "Lula doesn't even remember the last time he went grocery shopping because he lives in a luxury palace now." The two candidates mostly limited the discussion to pre-established themes in the first few segments of the debate, toning down the [USN:L6N46406G TEXT:"personal attacks"] that marked the only previous debate in the campaign between the two. At one point, Bolsonaro apologized to Lula after saying the president gives to Brazilians with one hand but "takes away with nine fingers." Lula lost his left little finger in an accident while working as a lathe operator in a factory. "I will not accept some rich guy, with a highly questionable political practice, calling me 'nine fingers,'" the incumbent said, demanding a retraction. "Lula, if I offended you by calling you 'nine fingers,' then I sincerely apologize, I sincerely apologize," Bolsonaro said. But he added: "Will you apologize to Brazilians suffering from insecurity ... in debt?" The discussion heated up in the last minutes of the debate, when both candidates were allowed to interact without moderation, as Lula and Bolsonaro sought to link each other to the fraud involving lender Banco Master. Lula pressed Bolsonaro on [USN:L1N4530F5 TEXT:"alleged links"] to the bank's jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro, and Bolsonaro questioned Lula [USN:L1N43X02G TEXT:"about accusations"] involving his son and a pension fraud. The debate was one of the campaign's final events, as Brazilian electoral law bars the candidates from broadcasting radio and TV campaign advertising starting on Saturday. They can still hold rallies until the final hours of the day.

item.title: Fire devastates former Nazi guest house 'Eagle's Nest'
item.description: Firefighters battled for hours to contain a blaze that engulfed the former Nazi guest house known as "The Eagle's Nest" in southern Germany, while police investigated the cause after detaining a man near the scene, authorities said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Firefighters battled for hours to contain a blaze that engulfed the former Nazi guest house known as "The Eagle's Nest" in southern Germany, while police investigated the cause after detaining a man near the scene, authorities said on Saturday. Around 200 firefighters and emergency workers near Berchtesgaden in Bavaria were battling the flames after the building, known as the Kehlsteinhaus, caught fire on Friday, police said. Built in 1938 as a guest house for Nazi officials and their guests, the building sits in a spectacular Alpine setting above Berchtesgaden. Adolf Hitler used it occasionally, earning it the nickname "Hitler's Tea House". It is separate from his nearby summer residence, the Berghof. Bild newspaper quoted a police spokesperson as saying the building, preserved after World War Two as a historical monument linked to the Nazi era, had been so badly damaged that it "could probably not be saved". Police said earlier they had detained a man near the site but had not yet established the cause of the fire. "Whether the person is linked to the fire is currently the subject of a criminal investigation," Bavarian police said in a statement.

item.title: Typhoon Champi sweeps past Taiwan, leaving 1 dead, 500 injured
item.description: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday, killing 1 person and injuring more than 500, downing trees and severing power, as it continued to weaken and head north towards the Chinese coast though it was not expected to make landfall there.
item.dc:creator: Yimou Lee, Angie Teo, Ann Wang
item.content:encoded: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday, killing 1 person and injuring more than 500, downing trees and severing power, as it continued to weaken and head north towards the Chinese coast though it was not expected to make landfall there. At one point a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year, Champi is weakening though still packing gusts of around 126 kph (78 mph) near its centre, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration. The storm was about 170 km (106 miles) northeast of Taiwan, having glanced off the island's northeastern coast in Yilan County early on Saturday, the CWA said. The centre of the storm turned south around midnight, hugging the Yilan coastline before making a rare loop offshore and moving away northward. Wind gusts touched 227 kph (141 mph) in some coastal areas, knocking down power lines and sending roof tiles flying. 'MOST TERRIFYING AROUND MIDNIGHT' "It was most terrifying around midnight," said a retired teacher surnamed Lin as he inspected downed banana trees in his garden in Yilan. "It was a sleepless night. I haven't seen anything like this in many years." The storm's forecast track shows it turning north, tracking up the Chinese coast and eventually moving into southern Japan. Taiwan's fire department said the death toll remained at 1, a man swept away by waves from the island of Liuqiu, with 527 injuries during the heavy wind and torrential rain. Taipower said more than 288,000 homes had lost electricity, though most had been reconnected. The transport ministry said 259 flights were cancelled, an improvement from Friday, when the number was almost 1,000. In the capital Taipei, there were downed trees and on-off squally rain showers. Taipei resident Thomas Wang, 70, said the storm felt like something out of the horror film "Poltergeist". "It was quite scary," he said, out running morning errands. Governments in a swathe of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second day of office and school closures on Saturday. Although more common in summer, typhoons can strike in autumn too. China's emergency management ministry sent a team to the eastern province of Zhejiang as Champi approached, warning of strong winds and heavy rain through Sunday. It said it had readied 400 rescue workers and 600 pieces of equipment, while more than 41,000 firefighters were on emergency duty. In Taizhou, a city on Zhejiang's coast, more than 3,800 fishing boats returned to harbour, offshore fish-farm workers were brought ashore and 2,084 island visitors were evacuated, state media reported. Authorities halted 25 offshore construction projects and suspended 18 passenger ferry routes.

item.title: Hot-shooting Hawks set franchise mark with 47-point rout of Hornets
item.description: Jalen Johnson and reserve Aaron Wiggins each scored 19 points as visiting Atlanta blew out the Charlotte Hornets 128-81 on Friday, the biggest margin of victory in Hawks history.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Jalen Johnson and reserve Aaron Wiggins each scored 19 points as visiting Atlanta blew out the Charlotte Hornets 128-81 on Friday, the biggest margin of victory in Hawks history. The 47-point gap topped the old record of 46 points set in a 126-80 victory over the visiting Sacramento Kings on Nov 15, 2017. Nickeil Alexander-Walker put up 14 points, CJ McCollum posted 13 points, Dyson Daniels contributed 11 points and nine rebounds and Corey Kispert also had 11 points for Atlanta, which won its second game in a row to start the season. Onyeka Okongwu added 10 points as the Hawks shot 50.5% from the field. Johnson supplied eight assists. It was a miserable home opener for the Hornets, who won two nights earlier at Brooklyn to start their campaign. They committed 27 turnovers. Naz Reid scored 17 points for Charlotte and Grayson Allen came off the bench for 11 points. Both players were in their home debuts with the Hornets. Reserve Tidjane Salaun also scored 11 points. The Hawks were efficient on offense throughout the game. The gap reached 97-62 by the end of the third quarter. The Hornets couldn't even get it cranked up when the margin was out of hand, needing about 6 1/2 minutes to reach a double-digit total in the fourth quarter. Wiggins, who shot 7-for-9 from the field, hit 3 of 5 from 3-point range. Charlotte's Brandon Miller finished 2-for-14 from the field, including 1-for-11 on 3-point tries. He scored six points. The Hornets didn't apply much pressure, not attempting a 10th free throw until deep into the fourth quarter. Atlanta built a 15-point first-quarter lead. It was 33-20 through the opening quarter, with the Hornets willing to fire away from the perimeter. Charlotte was 2-for-15 on first-quarter 3-point attempts. The Hawks poured it on in the second quarter to claim a 68-43 halftime lead on the strength of Wiggins' 15 points along with 13 points apiece from Johnson and McCollum. Atlanta benefited from Charlotte's 14 first-half turnovers. The Hornets played again without injured Kon Knueppel (hamstring), Coby White (calf) and Grant Williams (hamstring). --Field Level Media

item.title: PHP Foundation 'under-funded' with one full-time staff member, director says
item.description: The PHP project is receiving nearly twice as many proposed code changes as a year ago, yet the number of contributors hasn't doubled, Elizabeth Barron said.
item.dc:creator: Toby Sterling
item.content:encoded: The discovery of two serious flaws in PHP this week set off a global scramble to keep websites [USN:L1N468095 TEXT:"safe from hackers, "]showing just how critical the three-decade-old open-source programming language is to the internet. Yet the nonprofit foundation that supports PHP, which may underpin up to 70% of sites globally, operates on a shoestring budget. “We have one full-time staff member (that's me) and 14 mostly part-time contractors,” Executive Director Elizabeth Barron of the PHP Foundation said via email in an interview on Friday. Board members are unpaid volunteers, and funding comes from donations and grants. The foundatio.n works with outside researchers and companies, including OpenAI and cybersecurity firms Wiz and Calif, to investigate security flaws and coordinate fixes, including Wednesday's patches. While Web security company Cloudflare has reported millions of hacking attempts, Barron said the foundation had no evidence hackers were able to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were disclosed, or on sites that have been patched. "We received no further indication from OpenAI, Wiz or Calif, with whom we're working closely on this issue, regarding any issues on patched systems,” she said. Artificial intelligence has proved both a help and a burden to the foundation. It helped researchers find the flaws, which had been present for a decade, and Barron said it made programmers more efficient. However, it is also increasing maintainers' workloads. The PHP project is receiving nearly twice as many proposed code changes as a year ago, “yet the number of contributors hasn't doubled,” she said. Reviewing contributions and bug reports requires “a massive amount of human input and experience.” Recent events have shown how heavily companies and governments rely on PHP, Barron said. “Given that reliance, it is clear that PHP is incredibly under-funded.”

item.title: AI-discovered bugs may soon trigger fresh disruptions, cyber experts say
item.description: We spoke to seven cybersecurity professionals to learn more.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, A.J. Vicens
item.content:encoded: Advances in artificial intelligence have uncovered a stream of new software vulnerabilities that are almost certain to trigger more disruption along the lines of [USN:FWN4661WD TEXT:"the outages that percolated"] across global government websites this week, according to seven cybersecurity professionals who spoke to Reuters. AI helped drive a doubling of the number of digital flaws discovered year-on-year, according to research due to be published in the coming days by VulnCheck, a Massachusetts-based threat intelligence firm. Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the digital infrastructure firm Cloudflare (NET.N) , told Reuters he was aware of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software” and predicted busy months ahead as AI surfaced long-hidden weaknesses in the fabric of the internet. “I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling,” Prince said in an interview on Thursday. The outages that spread across government sites in Europe and elsewhere beginning on Wednesday happened after the discovery of weaknesses in PHP, a venerable programming language that powers a huge swath of the internet. Operators have been rushing to fix their software in anticipation of mass exploitation and, because some felt they could not patch before hackers jumped in, a subset simply [USN:L4N46716K TEXT:"yanked their sites offline"] until they could make them safe. VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity said the scramble to fix PHP came during an already busy week in cybersecurity. The week also brought disclosures of vulnerabilities PHP alternative Node.js and streaming program Plex, breaches tied to AI gateway LiteLLM and development platform Railway, and the revelation that the Indian certificate authority eMudhra had used [USN:L6N4680UW TEXT:"an extraordinarily flimsy cryptographic key"] that potentially put users across the internet at risk. “If we just saw four or five things like this, this week, I would expect we’re going to see a lot more,” Garrity said. “I think there’s going to be a lot more fire drills for anything that’s internet exposed.” TIMELINES SHORTENING The codebases that run modern programs are sprawling and mistakes, or “bugs,” that open up potential avenues for exploitation often crop up in unexpected places. Previously, finding bugs required a baseline level of skill, and taking advantage of those bugs to build digital lockpicks – called “exploits” – could be expected to take weeks or months of work by an experienced professional. That would in the past have provided defenders a little breathing room to fix bugs and gently roll out software updates. AI has effectively thrown those assumptions [USN:L6N42I12G TEXT:"out the window"]. Models can find one bug after another by subjecting codebases to round-the-clock scrutiny, and can turn around exploits in hours. Shane Fry, the chief technology officer of Virginia-based RunSafe Security, said the demonstrated performance of AI models over the past few months had effectively laid to rest any doubts over whether they would change the industry. “What's fundamentally, and unquestionably, changing is the timescale for not only finding vulnerabilities, but how quickly adversaries can weaponize them,” Fry said. SCARY MONSTERS While all the experts Reuters spoke to agreed that defenders’ timelines were getting shorter, they were split on whether AI would lead to a hacker free-for-all. Daniel Stenberg, the lead developer of the file transfer tool curl, argued the vulnerabilities found by AI models tended to be exotic bugs that were difficult for rogue actors to take advantage of. Ramy Rahman, a senior principal solutions engineer at cybersecurity company ArmorCode, said “more disclosed vulnerabilities do not automatically mean more successful attacks." There was tentative evidence of that around the PHP vulnerability that drew worldwide concern this week. Threat intelligence firm Hunt.io said that – like Amazon (AMZN.O) and Cloudflare – it had seen aggressive attempts to take advantage of the bug. But the firm’s head of research, Esteban Borges, said that, as of 2 p.m. Eastern Time on Thursday (1800 GMT), the cybercriminals he tracked appeared to have failed to cobble together a working tool to take advantage of it. Prince, of Cloudflare, told Reuters he had seen anecdotal evidence of compromises linked to the PHP vulnerability. The deluge of AI-driven discoveries might rattle the industry, but would be a net positive in the end, he said, comparing it to slaying the monsters in a haunted house. The confrontation might be scary, he said, but leaving the monsters to lurk quietly behind closed doors was far worse. “The reality is, we’re going to get a lot of this stuff cleaned up,” he said.

item.title: Israeli settlers steal Palestinians' olives as attacks on harvest grow more violent
item.description: Even when Palestinians can access their trees, it is not without risk.
item.dc:creator: Pesha Magid, Lina Obeid
item.content:encoded: Brought to tears as he recalled Israeli settlers hitting his cherished olive trees with sticks and taking off with the olives, Palestinian Ahmed Salem said he feared being attacked if he tried to intervene. Settlers have intimidated Palestinians harvesting their olives in the occupied West Bank for decades, but this year, not only has [USN:L8N4620II TEXT:"violence increased sharply"], theft has been widespread, according to Palestinians, Israeli rights groups and the UN. The settlers dumped Salem's olives into sacks and then drove them to a nearby Israeli settler outpost to be pressed into olive oil, the 50-year-old Palestinian told Reuters of the incident around two weeks ago near his village Lubban al-Gharbi. "How would you feel if something that belonged to you was being violated, and you could do nothing about it?" he asked. The couple living in the outpost, whose olive press settlers have urged Israelis to use for West Bank olives, declined multiple Reuters requests for comment, while the Yesha Council, which oversees Israeli settlements in the West Bank, did not immediately respond. The attacks have accelerated ahead of an Israeli election next week that opinion polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his pro-settler coalition could lose to opponents who have taken a [USN:L6N4660BW TEXT:"more critical stance"] against settler violence. 'SETTLERS CAN COME AND GO FREELY' The olive harvest starts with the onset of cooler weather, allowing Palestinian families to gather in the lush, terraced groves that they have groomed for generations. "My six-year-old son remembers going there with me, eating there, making tea there," Salem said. With the establishment of hundreds of small settler outposts under Netanyahu's government since 2022, the military has increasingly restricted Palestinian access to areas nearby, including many olive groves. "This creates a situation where Palestinians, in many of the cases, many of the lands, especially in proximity to settlements and outposts, cannot enter the land and harvest the trees," said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Israeli rights group Yesh Din. "But settlers can come and go freely, and that's what they do." Even when Palestinians can access their trees, it is not without risk. Yesh Din on Wednesday reported 125 physical attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters over the 24 days since the season began and 168 incidents of crop theft, with Israeli military forces present in at least a quarter of cases. An Israeli military official said it takes [USN:L6N46304S TEXT:"acts of violence"], criminal activity and attempts to undermine security very seriously. The official did not refer to settlers or comment on the reports of olive theft in the presence of the Israeli military, which has separately [USN:L8N45F1FN TEXT:"uprooted trees with excavators"], citing what it said was a need to prevent Palestinian attacks. The removal of Palestinians' olives has met with widely differing responses from Israeli rabbis. "I call it theft. From my perspective, I define it as theft or robbery, and it is forbidden," said Zev Weitman, the rabbi for the Alon Shvut settlement south of Bethlehem. Prominent Orthodox rabbi Dov Lior said settlers should harvest across the West Bank, asserting in an open letter that Palestinians had no ownership rights to the land and that harvesting olives fulfilled "the commandment of conquering the land." 'IT'S EITHER US OR OUR ENEMY', SETTLERS SAY ON SOCIAL MEDIA Hundreds of acres of the land around Salem's village, Lubban al-Gharbi, including olive groves, were fenced off and seized between 2023 and 2026 by Avichai Farm, an Israeli settler outpost built on a nearby hill. Salem said villagers have seen settlers harvest olives from the seized land and take them to the outpost's olive press. At the start of the olive harvest, settlers posted on social media calling on Israelis to harvest West Bank olives and bring them to Avichai Farm's press. "Both fine oil and strengthening the Jewish hold on the vast expanses of our land!," read a message on a settler Telegram group. "It's either us or our enemy!" The press at Avichai Farm advertises "premium products produced by Avichai Farm" with olive oil at about $20 a bottle via a website run by the Farms Association, a settler group that Reuters has reported receives significant financial support from the Israeli government, which says the aim is to promote peace. The Farms Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment and the couple who live on the farm with their children declined to be interviewed by a Reuters reporter who approached the area on Sunday. On a road leading to Avichai Farm, Reuters spoke to a man who declined to be identified and said he had driven from a settlement around 90 minutes away to press 14 bags of olives from trees he said he grew himself. Lubban al-Gharbi villagers and other Palestinians who have lost land to settler expansion say the harvesting of olives from trees in groves seized from Palestinian land constitutes theft. UN bodies and most countries deem Israel's settlements on land occupied in war illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied. 'WE PAY IN BLOOD FOR THE OLIVES' During this year's olive harvest, Palestinian authorities say three Palestinians have been killed in daily militant settler attacks, which have also injured several journalists, [USN:L6N46304S TEXT:"European diplomats and a French mayor"]. Stahl from the Yesh Din Israeli rights group said the violence was "part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing, paving the way for the annexation of the West Bank without its Palestinian population." Israel, which has [USN:L1N3W407X TEXT:"considered the idea of annexation"], said it is investigating some of the incidents. An Israeli government spokesperson said olives "picked by a Jew in the ancestral homeland of the Jewish people" did not constitute theft and that Jews owned and cultivated "millions of olive trees" in the area. No one should take the law into their own hands, the spokesperson added. Palestinian farmer Samer Ben Shamsi said masked settlers attacked him on October 9 in the Palestinian village of Beita near Nablus, then sped away in a pickup truck with his harvest of olives after he and other farmers fled. "This year, they steal without fear because they have a state and a powerful force backing them," Ben Shamsi said, referring to the security forces. Within the past year alone, settlers had shot him in the leg, beaten him and smashed his possessions, he said. "We pay in blood for the olives."

item.description: Allemagne-Le "nid d'aigle" des nazis en Bavière incendié
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Allemagne-Le "nid d'aigle" des nazis en Bavière incendié Le "nid d'aigle", ancienne résidence des dignitaires du régime nazi dans les montagnes bavaroises du sud de l'Allemagne, a pris feu vendredi soir et un suspect a été arrêté, a annoncé la police allemande. Le dirigeant nord-coréen Kim Jong Un en visite en Chine SEOUL, 24 octobre (Reuters) - Le dirigeant de la Corée du Nord Kim Jong Un s'est rendu samedi en Chine en empruntant un pont tout juste ouvert entre les deux pays, a-t-on appris d'un responsable gouvernemental sud-coréen. L'Ukraine dit que Starlink/Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à plus de 400 km/h KYIV, 24 octobre (Reuters) - Le système de communication par satellites Starlink et sa version militaire Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à des vitesses supérieures à 400 km/h, a déclaré samedi le ministre ukrainien de la Défense. La Russie et l'Ukraine acceptent un cessez-le-feu à Oleshky La Russie et l'Ukraine ont accepté de respecter un cessez-le-feu dans la ville ukrainienne d'Oleshky, occupée par la Russie, afin de permettre l'évacuation des civils pris au piège des combats, a annoncé vendredi la Maison blanche. L'Autriche expulse quatre diplomates russes, Moscou promet de répliquer Le ministère autrichien des Affaires étrangères a annoncé vendredi l'expulsion de quatre diplomates russes basés à Vienne en raison "d'activités incompatibles avec leur statut diplomatique", expression généralement employée pour des faits d'espionnage. La Corée du Sud propose à nouveau de discuter avec la Corée du Nord de la frontière terrestre Le ministère sud-coréen de la Défense a de nouveau proposé vendredi la tenue de pourparlers militaires avec la Corée du Nord, afin de s'accorder sur le tracé exact de la frontière terrestre entre les deux Corées et de réduire le risque d'affrontements accidentels. Le séisme au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés Le séisme de magnitude 7 survenu au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés, a annoncé vendredi le gouvernement local sur les réseaux sociaux. Les plus anciennes peintures rupestres du monde menacées par les feux de forêt Les plus anciennes peintures rupestres du monde, situées sur l'île indonésienne de Sulawesi, sont menacées par la chaleur et la fumée générées par les pires feux de forêt que le pays ait connus depuis plus d'une décennie, ont déclaré des chercheurs. Arabie saoudite: Nouveau report de forums internationaux à 2027 Deux nouveaux forums internationaux prévus en cette fin d'année en Arabie saoudite ont été reportés à 2027 en raison des attaques que lancent les Houthis, rebelles yéménites proches de l'Iran, sur le royaume, a déclaré vendredi l'Autorité générale des statistiques du pays. Une nappe de pétrole détectée au large des Emirats arabes unis Une nappe de pétrole émanant d'un pétrolier a été détectée dans le Golfe au large de l'émirat d'Oumm al Qaïwaïn, a annoncé vendredi le ministère de l'Environnement des Emirats arabes unis, qui a ordonné la fermeture temporaire des plages de la région afin de procéder à une évaluation des dégâts et de prendre des mesures de protection des zones affectées.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La garde à vue du suspect de l'attaque de Trappes prolongée PARIS, 24 octobre (Reuters) - La garde à vue du suspect de l'attaque commise vendredi dans les Yvelines, qui a fait un mort et quatre blessés graves, dont une fillette de 12 ans, a été prolongée, a annoncé samedi le parquet national antiterroriste (PNAT). Jordan Bardella reconduit à la présidence du Rassemblement national ORLÉANS, Loiret, 24 octobre (Reuters) - Jordan Bardella a été reconduit samedi à la présidence du Rassemblement national, premier parti d'opposition de France, lors d'un congrès à Orléans (Loiret) où des personnalités de gauche ont participé de leur côté à une manifestation hostile à l'extrême droite. Veillée d'armes avant une nouvelle journée de manifestations, le dispositif sécuritaire renforcé La France se préparait vendredi à une nouvelle journée de manifestations à hauts risques samedi, une semaine après les violences et les pillages survenus en marge de défilés pour les conditions d'enseignement détériorées et contre la vie chère, obligeant l'exécutif à un sursaut. Le Pnat saisi après des tirs dans les Yvelines, sur place Macron dénonce un acte terroriste raciste Le président Emmanuel Macron s'est rendu à Trappes, dans les Yvelines, l'une des communes où un homme à bord d'un véhicule a tiré vendredi à l'arme automatique sur la voie publique, faisant un mort et quatre blessés graves, dont une fille de 12 ans. La tempête Austen balaie l'ouest de la France, 161.000 foyers privés d'électricité Quelque 161.000 foyers étaient privés d'électricité vendredi matin dans l'ouest de la France balayé par la tempête Austen, la première de l'automne, qui s'accompagne de vents violents, rapporte Enedis. Macron annonce l'interdiction des manifestations "sans légitimité" Les autorités interdiront dans les prochains jours les manifestations et regroupements sans "légitimité" et proposeront des "tracés alternatifs" aux syndicats pour protéger les centre-villes, a annoncé jeudi Emmanuel Macron, à deux jours d'un nouvel appel à manifester émanant notamment des "gilets jaunes". France: Premier décès lié au virus Shamonda, aucun risque sanitaire à ce jour selon les autorités Un patient est décédé début octobre du virus de Shamonda, une première en France et dans le monde, a annoncé jeudi le gouvernement, ajoutant qu'il n'y avait à ce stade aucun risque sanitaire pour la population générale au vu des connaissances sur ce virus. Cisjordanie: Les oliveraies de Palestiniens pillées lors d'attaques violentes de colons israéliens Ému aux larmes en se remémorant l'attaque contre son oliveraie par des colons israéliens il y a environ deux semaines près du village palestinien de Lubban al-Gharbi, en Cisjordanie, Ahmed Salem a déclaré s'être retrouvé impuissant, craignant d'être agressé s'il tentait d'intervenir pour protéger son exploitation. Gaza: Trois Palestiniens tués par des frappes israéliennes selon les secours Des frappes et des tirs israéliens ont tué au moins trois Palestiniens jeudi, dans deux incidents séparés survenus dans la bande Gaza, selon les autorités sanitaires locales. Serbie: La face autoritaire de Vucic en lumière avant les élections législatives Le militant serbe Marko Marjanovic rentrait du supermarché à Belgrade lorsque des officiers masqués l'ont embarqué dans un véhicule avant de l'amener dans le sous-sol d'un commissariat de police où il a été maintenu à l'isolement pendant deux jours sous un éclairage intense.
